screens.title: A floor under each leaf
screens.prose: Depth is one control. `min_samples_leaf` is another: every leaf must hold at least that many training rows. `min_samples_split` says a node needs that many rows before it may split at all.
screens.question: With `min_samples_leaf=20` on 300 rows, what is the largest number of leaves possible?

hints.text: Every training row ends in exactly one leaf.
Each leaf needs at least 20 of the 300 rows.
$300 / 20 = 15$ leaves at most.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide the rows by the smallest number a leaf may hold.

byKey.twenty: 20 is the floor per leaf, not the number of leaves. Divide 300 by it.
byKey.split: Leaves share the 300 rows. Each holds at least 20, so there are at most 15.

explain.text: The fitted tree has 10 leaves, inside the cap of 15. Its test accuracy is 77%, against 66% for the unlimited tree. A floor on leaf size stops the tree drawing rectangles around one or two loans.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check whether any split could leave 151 rows on each side.

byKey.stump: A stump needs two leaves of at least 151 rows, 302 in all. With 300 rows the root cannot split.

widget.prelude:
import numpy as np

def make_loans(seed, n=400):
    """n loans: [leverage, interest cover], outcome 1 = default, 0 = repaid.
    Defaults cluster where leverage > 3.5 and cover < 3, or cover < 1.5."""
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    lev = np.round(rng.uniform(0.5, 6.0, n), 2)
    cover = np.round(rng.uniform(0.5, 8.0, n), 2)
    p = np.where(lev > 3.5, np.where(cover < 3.0, 0.8, 0.3), np.where(cover < 1.5, 0.5, 0.08))
    y = (rng.random(n) < p).astype(int)
    return np.column_stack([lev, cover]), y

def make_one_threshold(seed, n=300):
    """Loans whose default risk depends on one threshold: leverage > 3.5."""
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    lev = np.round(rng.uniform(0.5, 6.0, n), 2)
    cover = np.round(rng.uniform(0.5, 8.0, n), 2)
    p = np.where(lev > 3.5, 0.85, 0.1)
    y = (rng.random(n) < p).astype(int)
    return np.column_stack([lev, cover]), y

widget.solution:
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier

def train_test_acc_by_depth(X_train, y_train, X_test, y_test, depths):
    train_acc, test_acc = [], []
    for d in depths:
        model = DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=d, random_state=0).fit(X_train, y_train)
        train_acc.append(round(float(model.score(X_train, y_train)), 4))
        test_acc.append(round(float(model.score(X_test, y_test)), 4))
    return train_acc, test_acc

screens.title: Choosing depth with the test set
screens.prose: A colleague fits depths 1 to 15, keeps depth 2 because its test accuracy is best, and reports 81.5% as the accuracy to expect on next year's loans.
screens.question: What is wrong with the 81.5%?

options.text: It is optimistic: the test set chose the depth, so it no longer measures unseen data
Nothing: test data was never used for fitting
options.why: No tree was fitted on it, but it picked the winner among 15 trees. A choice made on the test set leaks into its score.

options.text: It is too low: deeper trees would do better live
options.why: The deep trees did worse on test data. The problem is the opposite: the best of 15 test scores flatters.

options.text: Accuracy is the wrong metric for a tree
options.why: Accuracy is a fair metric here. The issue is which rows chose the depth.

hints.text: Which data did the choice of depth look at?
Picking the best of 15 test scores rewards luck on those 200 loans.
Choose depth on the training rows by cross-validation, then score the test set once.

feedback.correct: Once the test set picks the model, its score is no longer honest.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask which rows decided the depth.

byKey.fine: You tuned depth on the test set. Its best score is partly luck in those 200 loans, so it overstates live accuracy.

explain.text: Picking the best of 15 test scores rewards the depth that happened to suit those 200 loans. The honest route, from the validation course: choose depth by cross-validation on the training rows, then score the test set once.

screens.title: Pruning: grow, then cut
screens.prose: **Cost-complexity pruning** grows the full tree, then cuts back. It scores a tree by its total impurity plus $\alpha$ per leaf: $C_\alpha(T) = R(T) + \alpha\,|T|$. A branch is cut when its impurity saving no longer pays for its extra leaves.

state.caption: $R$ is weighted impurity. As one leaf the branch has $R = 0.040$; its three leaves add to $0.012 + 0 + 0$.

screens.question: Cutting the branch to one leaf saves 2 leaves and costs $0.040 - 0.012 = 0.028$ of impurity. Above what $\alpha$ is the cut worth it?

widget.label: Alpha at which pruning breaks even

hints.text: The cut removes 2 leaves and adds $0.028$ of impurity.
It pays when $\alpha \times 2$ exceeds $0.028$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide the impurity cost by the number of leaves the cut removes.

byKey.nodiv: That is the impurity cost. Spread it over the 2 leaves saved.
byKey.three: The branch has 3 leaves but becomes 1, so it saves 2, not 3.

explain.text: Cut when $\alpha \cdot 2 > 0.028$, so $\alpha > 0.014$. scikit-learn computes this break-even $\alpha$ for every branch and cuts the weakest first. As $\alpha$ rises, the tree shrinks towards a single leaf.

screens.title: Pruning in scikit-learn
screens.prose: `cost_complexity_pruning_path` lists the break-even alphas of the full tree. Passing `ccp_alpha=alpha` to the tree prunes every branch whose break-even is at most `alpha`.
screens.question: Complete `leaves_at_alpha` so it returns the number of leaves after pruning at `alpha`.

screens.title: Same loans, different tree
screens.prose: Draw 120 loans at random, with replacement, from the 120 training loans, and fit a depth-2 tree. Then draw again. These are the two trees from two such samples.
screens.question: What does this say about a single deep tree?

options.text: It has high variance: a small change in the data changes the whole tree
It has high bias: it cannot fit the data
options.why: Unlimited, it fits every training loan. Its weakness is instability, not rigidity.

options.text: One of the samples must be faulty
options.why: Both are fair samples of the same 120 loans. The tree itself is what swings.

options.text: Only the root question is unstable; the rest is fixed
options.why: The questions below the root changed too, because each depends on which loans reached that node.

hints.text: Compare the root questions.
Sample 1 asks about leverage first; sample 2 asks about cover.
Same population, different questions all the way down: the fitted tree swings with the sample.

feedback.correct: High variance, low bias: the deep tree's signature.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The two samples came from the same loans; what changed?

explain.text: Sample 1's tree starts with *leverage ≤ 2.03*, sample 2's with *cover ≤ 3.18*. Grown to full depth they have 23 and 21 leaves. A deep tree is low bias, high variance; level 2 averages many such trees to cancel the variance.

screens.title: Fourteen conditions
screens.prose: A researcher fits an unlimited tree to 300 trading days. One leaf is a rule with 14 nested conditions, and on its days the strategy never lost. Suppose each condition keeps about half of the days that reach it.
screens.question: About how many of the 300 days would satisfy all 14 conditions?

hints.text: Each condition halves the days.
After 14 halvings, 300 becomes $300 / 2^{14}$.

feedback.correct: Far less than one day: the rule describes one or two particular days.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Halve 300 fourteen times.

byKey.lin: You divided by 14. Each condition halves what is left, so divide by $2^{14}$.
byKey.half: That is one condition. There are 14.

explain.text: Halving 14 times leaves about 0.02 days, so the leaf can only exist by fitting one or two real days exactly. Its 100% hit rate is memorised noise and will not survive live trading. Desks prefer depth 2 or 3: each leaf holds about 40 to 75 days and the rule can be stated aloud.

ideas: An unlimited tree reaches 100% training accuracy by giving single rows their own leaves; its test error follows a U-shape in depth.
max_depth, min_samples_leaf, min_samples_split and ccp_alpha limit growth; choose them by cross-validation, never on the test set.
A deep tree is low bias and high variance: resample the rows and its questions change all the way down.

formula.name: Cost-complexity pruning
formula.note: $R$ is the weighted impurity of the leaves, $|T|$ the number of leaves.

summary.trap: Choosing the depth with the test set, which makes the reported test score optimistic.

quiz.prose: After pruning at $\alpha = 0.01$ a tree's training accuracy falls from 100% to 79%. A colleague wants to undo the pruning.
quiz.question: What should you check before deciding?

options.text: Accuracy on held-out rows: the pruned tree scored 80.5% on test against 66%
Nothing: lower training accuracy means a worse model
options.why: You read training accuracy as skill. Pruning is meant to lower it; only held-out accuracy can judge the cut.

options.text: That the tree still has at least 10 leaves
options.why: No leaf count is right in itself. Judge the tree on rows it did not see.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Which accuracy can tell memorising from learning?

explain.text: A pruned tree fits its training rows worse by design. On the 200 test loans it scored 80.5% against the full tree's 66%. Keep the pruning.

quiz.prose: An unlimited tree and a depth-1 stump are fitted to the same 300 loans.
quiz.question: Which description fits each?

options.text: Unlimited: low bias, high variance. Stump: high bias, low variance
Unlimited: high bias, low variance. Stump: low bias, high variance
options.why: You swapped them. The unlimited tree fits anything, so its bias is low; it swings with the sample.

options.text: Both low bias, since trees can fit any shape
options.why: Only a deep tree can. A stump draws one line, so it misses most shapes.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Which tree could fit any pattern, and which changes most with the sample?

explain.text: A deep tree can carve any region, so its bias is low, but each sample gives a different tree. A stump barely changes between samples but cannot bend to the data.

quiz.prose: A tree has `min_samples_split=10`. A node holds 9 training loans: 5 defaults and 4 repaid.
quiz.question: What does the tree do at this node?

options.text: It makes the node a leaf predicting default
It splits, since the node is not pure
options.why: The node has fewer than 10 rows, so it may not split, pure or not.

options.text: It merges the node with its sibling
options.why: Trees never merge nodes while growing; a node that cannot split becomes a leaf.

feedback.correct: Too few rows to split: it is a leaf.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare the node's size with `min_samples_split`.

explain.text: `min_samples_split=10` forbids splitting nodes with fewer than 10 rows. The node becomes a leaf and predicts its majority, default, 5 to 4.

quiz.prose: Default risk in a loan book depends only on whether leverage exceeds 3.5. You choose depth from 1 to 6 by cross-validation.
quiz.question: Which depth do you expect CV to choose?

options.text: Depth 1: one question captures the whole signal
Depth 6: more questions never hurt
options.why: Extra questions fit noise. On `make_one_threshold(2)` depth 6 scored 85.7% in CV against 89.3% for depth 1.

options.text: Depth 2: a tree needs two features
options.why: A tree may use one feature only. Cover carries no signal here.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. How many questions does the true rule need?

explain.text: The true rule is one threshold, so a stump at leverage 3.5 is the right model. Each further split fits noise and lowers CV accuracy: 89.3%, 89.0%, 87.0% for depths 1 to 3.
